title: Maryland Public Defender to lead new partnership on criminal justice reform
summary: The Maryland Public Defender's Office is forming a new partnership to transform the state's criminal justice system by implementing recommendations of another collaborative that was dissolved less than a month ago.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters December 15, 2025

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters December 15, 2025

The Maryland Public Defender’s Office is forming a new partnership to transform the state’s criminal justice system by implementing recommendations of another collaborative that was dissolved less than a month ago.

The Maryland Justice Partnership is schedule to launch on Jan. 12, just two days before the start of the 2026 General Assembly, to follow up on the work of the Maryland Equitable Justice Collaborative. That body, a historic joint effort of the public defender and the Maryland Attorney General’s Office, dissolved Nov. 26 after two years of work.

The main goal of that collaborative was to deliver recommendations on ending mass incarceration in a state where Blacks account for about 30% of the state’s population, but make up about 71% of the state’s prison population. It was disbanded after delivering a 100-page report in March that included statistics on disparities and recommended solutions.

At the time, the collaborative’s supporters said its work would continue. The new parthership’s goal is to come up with a plan to create solutions based on the collaborative’s recommendations.

Heather Warnken, executive director of the Center for Criminal Justice Reform at the University of Baltimore School of Law, said Monday she will be part of the partnership. Warnken served as co-chair of one work group on the justice collaborative and a member of three other work groups.

Attorney general, public defender dissolve historic ‘equitable justice’ collaborative

“The fact that this new vehicle will exist to focus on continuing … the partnerships needed not only to advance the recommendations but really be into the weeds into a collaborative way on what it takes to implement them effectively,” Warnken said. “Public safety exists in so many different forums. It takes so many different partners to each have a distinct role to play.”

Similar to the collaborative, the justice partnership seeks to involve other stakeholders, such as state agencies, nonprofit organizations and community leaders as part of the reform initiatives. Participation in the justice partnership is voluntary.

The public defender’s office, which announced the formation of its partnership last Tuesday, plans to incorporate six hubs:

The office says this initiative will serve differently from the collaborative to not only focus on implementing solutions, but also allowing “impacted communities” to lead alongside state agencies.

One of those individuals who wants to serve in the justice partnership is Gordon Pack, who was a member of the collaborative’s prison, jail and detention facility reform work group. Pack, who served 42 years in prison for various crimes he committed at age 15, said Monday he would like to work on dealing with ways to improve parole and probation.

“It gives us a space to continue the work that needs to be done,” he said.

One main theme the public defender’s office and advocates continue to push is stopping the state’s practice of automatically charging youth as adults.

That will translate into legislation for next year’s session expected to be filed again by Sen. William C. Smith Jr. (D-Montgomery), the chair of the Judicial Proceedings Committee.

Smith will reintroduce his bill, which didn’t advance beyond a Senate committee in 2025. It would have raised the age at which a youth could be tried as an adult, from 14 to 16. It also would have made those 16 and younger eligible for juvenile court if charged with certain crimes, including first-degree assault, third-degree sex offense and certain offenses involving firearms.

“We have studied the problem. We have documented the crisis. Now we must act,” Public Defender Natasha Dartigue said in a statement announcing the partership.

“OPD is uniquely positioned to lead because we witness the consequences of injustice every day – in every courtroom, with every client, in every community,” she said. “We will drive results and keep impacted communities at the center of every decision.”
